title: Words that aren't verbs
goal: Master active participles — a family of words that look like adjectives, work like verbs, and point to now or later even though they feel like they're about the past.
bekal: recognize and use the ten most common active participles
tell عارف from بعرف, and رايح from بروح
negate them with مش, not with the wrap

dialogs.title: حوار — على السلم
dialogs.intro: Budi runs into Umm Sayed on the stairs of the building. She is carrying two shopping bags.

lines.speaker: أم سيد:
lines.id: Budi! Where are you off to this late?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: رايح المحطة. مستني صاحبي جاي من الأقصر.
lines.baca: raayih il-mahaṭṭa. mistanni ṣaahbi gayy mil-U’ṣur.
lines.id: To the station. I'm waiting for a friend who's coming from Luxor.
lines.literal: going station. waiting my-friend coming from Luxor.

lines.speaker: أم سيد:
lines.id: Do you know the way? The station is a bit far.
lines.literal: and knowing the-way? the-station far a-little.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: I know. I've been there twice before.

lines.speaker: أم سيد:
lines.text: طيب. وحاطط الموبايل في جيبك؟ خلي بالك.
lines.baca: ṭayyib. wi haaṭiṭ il-mobaayl fi gēbak? khalli baalak.
lines.id: Good. And have you put your phone in your pocket? Be careful.
lines.literal: good. and putting the-phone in your-pocket? keep your-mind.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: شايله في الشنطة. مش حانسى المرة دي.
lines.baca: shaayilu fish-shanṭa. mish hansa l-marra di.
lines.id: I've got it in my bag. I won't forget it this time.
lines.literal: carrying-it in-the-bag. not I-will-forget the-time this.

lines.speaker: أم سيد:
lines.id: And where does this friend of yours live?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: لسه مش لاقي مكان. حينام عندي كام يوم.
lines.baca: lissa mish laa’i makaan. haynaam ‘andi kaam yōm.
lines.id: He hasn't found a place yet. He'll stay with me for a few days.
lines.literal: still not finding place. he-will-sleep at-me few days.

lines.speaker: أم سيد:
lines.text: أهلاً وسهلاً بيه. قوله البيت بيته.
lines.baca: ahlan wi sahlan biih. ’ullu il-bēt bētu.
lines.id: He's very welcome. Tell him our home is his home.
lines.literal: welcome and welcome with-him. tell-him the-house his-house.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: ربنا يخليكي يا حاجة. شايلة حاجات تقيلة؟
lines.baca: rabbina yikhalliiki ya haagga. shayla hagaat ti’iila?
lines.id: God keep you, ma'am. Are you carrying something heavy?
lines.literal: our-Lord keep-you O hajja. carrying things heavy?

lines.speaker: أم سيد:
lines.id: A bit. But I can manage, don't worry.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: لأ، أنا شايلهالك. الدور التاني صح؟
lines.baca: la’, ana shayilhaalik. id-dōr it-taani ṣahh?
lines.id: No, let me carry them for you. Second floor, right?
lines.literal: no, I carrying-it-for-you. the-floor the-second right?

lines.speaker: أم سيد:
lines.text: ربنا يكرمك يا ابني. انت طيب أوي.
lines.baca: rabbina yikrimak ya ibni. inta ṭayyib ’awi.
lines.id: God bless you, son. You're very kind.
lines.literal: our-Lord honor-you O my-son. you kind very.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: ده واجب. يلا، أنا متأخر شوية.
lines.baca: da waagib. yalla, ana mit’akhkhar shuwayya.
lines.id: It's nothing. Well, I'm running a bit late.
lines.literal: this duty. come-on, I late a-little.

lines.speaker: أم سيد:
lines.id: Go safely. And say hello to your friend.
lines.literal: go with-the-safety. and tell to-your-friend welcome.

notes: **Words like رايح، عارف، فاكر، ساكن are active participles.** They change form like adjectives — رايح، رايحة، رايحين — not by who does the action, as verbs do. They never take بـ and have no past form of their own.
**The confusing part: they feel finished, but they mean now or soon.** أنا رايح means "I'm on my way" or "I'm going to go", not "I've gone". For that you say أنا رحت.

**With verbs of motion, this form is actually more common than the verb itself.** رايح فين؟ is far more usual than بتروح فين؟ The second sounds like a question about habits: "where do you usually go?"
**For knowing and remembering, this is the only right form.** عارف and فاكر are what you use; بعرف and بفتكر are rare and mean something else. To say "I know", say أنا عارف, full stop.
**They are always negated with مش, never with the wrap.** مش عارف، مش فاكر، مش رايح. That makes sense, since none of them is a verb — just like مش طالب and مش كويس.

**The phrase خلي بالك means "be careful", literally "keep your mind".** You will hear it many times a day in Egypt, and it also means "pay close attention". To a woman it is spelled the same, خلي بالك, but said *khalli baalik*.
**The word واجب means "duty", and ده واجب is the standard reply to thanks for a favor.** It is like "it was nothing" in English: it turns down the praise without turning down the friendship.

grammars.title: The ten most common active participles
body: Each one has just three forms: masculine, feminine, and plural. No other forms at all.
after: Notice that the feminine often **shortens its first vowel**: رايح becomes رايحة, said *rayha*, not *raayiha*. The same happens in عارفة *‘arfa* and ساكنة *sakna*.
To put it in the past, just add كان in front: كنت رايح (I was on my way there), كانت مستنية (she was waiting). This is the same كان pattern from unit fourteen.
Object endings attach to it just as they do to verbs: مستنيك (waiting for you), شايلها (carrying it), فاكرني؟ (do you remember me?).

grammars.title: Participle or verb: عارف or بعرف, رايح or بروح
body: Some verbs have two forms that are both alive, and the difference is not grammar but meaning.
after: The first row is worth remembering: in Egyptian, بعرف means **"I can"**, not "I know". بعرف أسوق means "I can drive". Use it for knowledge and the meaning goes astray.

The last row shows that the بـ form marks **an action in progress**, while the active participle marks **the state that results from it**. لابس = already dressed and still wearing it; بلبس = putting it on.

head: مصري
Say it
Meaning
rows: where did you put the money?

blocks.text: The phrase مش عارف is one of the things you'll say most as a beginner, and it never sounds rude. To soften it even more: والله مش عارف (honestly, I don't know) — not a real oath, just an intensifier like "really".

blocks.title: Three look-alike words with extra meanings
items: The word قاعد means sitting, but also "being somewhere" or "just hanging around": قاعد في البيت (I'm at home), قاعد بعمل إيه؟ (what are you up to?).
The word واقف *waa’if* means standing, and also stopped: العربية واقفة (the car has stopped), الساعة واقفة (the clock has stopped).
The word نايم *naayim* means asleep, and also lying down. To wake someone up: صحي *ṣahhi*, and to say someone is asleep: هو نايم دلوقتي.

sections.title: Phrases that keep the day flowing

blocks.text: Most of the sentences in this unit's dialogue are short blessings. Egyptian uses them to oil everyday social life, and using them makes you sound instantly much warmer.

head: مصري
Say it
When to use it
rows: to whoever cooked or made something
turning down praise for a favor

blocks.text: The word نورت literally means "you've lit up (the place)", and it is said to anyone who has just walked into a home, office, or shop. The reply is المكان منور بيك ("the place is lit up by you"). This pair is one of the sweetest in Egyptian, and using it at the right moment always brings a smile.

vocab.en: welcome (lit. you've lit up the place)

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right form of the active participle.

items: Where are you off to this late?
I'm waiting for my friend who's coming from Luxor.
Do you know the way? (to a man)
He hasn't found a place to live yet.
Let me carry it for you.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: أنا مش عارف الطريق. — هي مش فاكرة الميعاد. — احنا مش رايحين النهاردة. — هو مش ساكن هنا. — أنا مش قادر أساعدك.
رايح فين بالليل كده؟ — مستني صاحبي جاي من الأقصر. — عارف الطريق؟ — لسه مش لاقي مكان. — أنا شايلهالك.
رايح فين بالليل كده؟ — أنا رايح المحطة. — مستني صاحبي جاي من الأقصر. — أنا عارف الطريق. — خلي بالك.
wave: Tomorrow, every time you're about to say "I know" or "I'm going", catch yourself and use عارف or رايح, not the form that starts with بـ.
